question: What is JSON and why is it the dominant data format for REST APIs?
title: JSON in REST APIs
direct_answer: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight text-based data format using key-value pairs, arrays, and nested objects. REST APIs use JSON because it's human-readable, language-agnostic, natively supported by browsers, and more compact than XML.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of JSON structure and why REST adopted it over alternatives like XML
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking JSON is JavaScript-only or not knowing the six primitive data types JSON supports
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention JSON's limitations like no date type or comments, and explain how Jackson's ObjectMapper handles these gaps in Spring Boot

sections.title: What JSON Is and Why REST APIs Chose It
sections.content:
**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is a **text-based data format** that structures information using **key-value pairs**, **arrays**, and **nested objects**. Despite the name, JSON is **language-agnostic** — every major programming language has libraries to parse and generate it.

Think of JSON as the universal language for APIs: when your Spring Boot backend talks to a React frontend or an Android app, JSON is the common ground. REST APIs adopted JSON over XML because it's **more compact** (30-40% smaller payloads), **human-readable** for debugging, and **natively supported by JavaScript**, making browser-based clients simpler. JSON supports six primitive types: **string**, **number**, **boolean**, **null**, **object**, and **array**. No comments, no date type, no binary data — which is both a simplicity win and a limitation you'll handle with conventions.

sections.title: JSON Structure Representing a Customer Order
When JSON Is the Right Choice
sections.content:
Use JSON for **web and mobile APIs** where clients are JavaScript-based browsers, iOS, or Android apps — it's the de facto standard.

Use JSON when you need **human-readable payloads** for debugging in tools like Postman or browser DevTools.

Use JSON when **payload size matters** — mobile clients on slow networks benefit from JSON's compactness compared to XML's verbose tags.

Avoid JSON for **binary data** like images or PDFs (use multipart/form-data or dedicated endpoints).

Avoid JSON when you need **strict schema validation** — consider Protocol Buffers or GraphQL for type-safe contracts.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking JSON is JavaScript-only**: Freshers assume JSON only works in JavaScript because of the name. JSON is a universal text format — Java, Python, Go, and every backend language parse it identically.
- **Not knowing JSON has no date type**: Freshers send dates as strings like "2024-01-15" without realizing JSON has no native date format. You must agree on a convention (ISO 8601 is standard) and handle parsing in Java with LocalDate or Instant.
- **Adding comments in JSON**: Freshers familiar with JavaScript try // comments in JSON files. JSON spec forbids comments — if you need documentation, use a separate schema file or API docs.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Six primitive types**: string, number, boolean, null, object, array — no date, no binary, no comments
**Language-agnostic**: despite the JavaScript name, JSON works identically in Java, Python, Go, and all major languages
**REST standard**: 90% of public REST APIs use JSON over XML because it's more compact and browser-friendly
**Human-readable**: you can open a JSON payload in a text editor and immediately understand the structure
**Case-sensitive keys**: "userId" and "userid" are different keys — JSON is case-sensitive for property names
**No trailing commas**: {"a":1,} is invalid JSON — a common mistake when hand-writing test data
**UTF-8 encoding**: JSON is always UTF-8, so international characters work natively without special handling

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: JSON is a lightweight text format that uses key-value pairs and arrays to structure data. It's the dominant format for REST APIs because it's human-readable, works with every programming language, and is natively supported by browsers. When your Spring Boot app sends data to a React frontend, JSON is the common language — compact and easy to debug. JSON supports six types: strings, numbers, booleans, null, objects, and arrays. That's it. No date type, no comments, no binary data. This simplicity makes JSON fast to parse but means you need conventions. For dates, we use ISO 8601 strings like two-thousand-twenty-four dash zero-one dash fifteen. Spring Boot's Jackson library handles the conversion automatically. One limitation is that JSON has no schema enforcement — you can send extra fields or miss required ones, and JSON itself won't complain. That's why we use Bean Validation annotations in Spring Boot to catch bad data. If you want to stand out, mention that JSON's lack of a date type means you configure Jackson to serialize LocalDateTime as ISO strings, not epoch milliseconds, so mobile clients can parse them easily.

question: How does Spring Boot serialize and deserialize JSON with Jackson?
title: Jackson JSON Serialization in Spring Boot
direct_answer: Spring Boot auto-configures Jackson as the default JSON processor. Methods in @RestController returning objects are automatically serialized to JSON. @RequestBody deserializes incoming JSON to Java objects. Jackson uses reflection and getter/setter conventions unless you customize with annotations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how Spring Boot handles JSON conversion automatically without explicit code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Jackson ignores unknown JSON fields by default, causing confusion when extra fields don't break deserialization
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain ObjectMapper configuration, mention @JsonProperty for field renaming, and discuss how to handle LocalDateTime serialization

sections.title: How Spring Boot and Jackson Work Together
sections.content:
Spring Boot includes **Jackson** as the default **JSON processor** through the spring-boot-starter-web dependency. When a method in a **@RestController** returns a Java object, Spring's **HttpMessageConverter** detects the response type and delegates to Jackson's **ObjectMapper**, which serializes the object to JSON using **reflection** and **getter methods**.

The reverse happens for **@RequestBody**: Jackson reads the incoming JSON string and constructs a Java object using the **default constructor** and **setter methods**. This all happens **automatically** — you don't write parsing code. Jackson follows **JavaBean conventions**: it looks for getFieldName() methods during serialization and setFieldName() during deserialization. If your class uses **records** (Java 17), Jackson uses the canonical constructor instead. You can customize behavior with annotations like **@JsonProperty** to rename fields or **@JsonIgnore** to exclude sensitive data like passwords.

sections.title: Jackson JSON Serialization in Spring Boot at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Jackson ObjectMapper|~the core engine that converts Java objects to JSON and vice versa using reflection
blue|@RestController|~automatically triggers JSON serialization — no need to manually call ObjectMapper in your code
emerald|@RequestBody|~tells Spring to deserialize the HTTP request JSON into the method parameter object
violet|JavaBean conventions|~Jackson uses getters for serialization and setters for deserialization by default
rose|Ignores unknown fields|~by default, extra JSON fields not in the Java class are silently ignored during deserialization
cyan|@JsonProperty|~renames a field in JSON (e.g., user_id in JSON maps to userId in Java)

sections.title: Automatic JSON Serialization and Deserialization
When You Need Custom Jackson Configuration
sections.content:
Use Jackson's default behavior for **standard DTOs** with simple types like String, Integer, Boolean — it just works. Customize with **@JsonProperty** when your API uses **snake_case** (like order_id) but your Java code uses **camelCase** (orderId) — mobile clients often expect snake_case. Customize with **@JsonIgnore** to exclude **sensitive fields** like password hashes or internal IDs from responses. Configure **ObjectMapper** globally when you need to handle **Java 8 date types** like LocalDateTime — Spring Boot's JavaTimeModule converts them to ISO 8601 strings automatically, but you might want epoch milliseconds for legacy clients.

Use **@JsonFormat** for custom date patterns like MM-dd-yyyy when integrating with legacy systems that don't support ISO 8601.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing Jackson ignores unknown fields**: Freshers panic when the client sends extra JSON fields not in the Java class. By default, Jackson ignores them — no error, no exception. If you want strict validation, configure ObjectMapper with FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES.
- **Missing default constructor**: Freshers create a class with only a parameterized constructor. Jackson can't deserialize because it needs a no-arg constructor to instantiate the object before calling setters. Records avoid this issue by using the canonical constructor.
- **Forgetting to add getters**: Freshers create private fields without getters. During serialization, Jackson finds no getters and returns empty JSON curly braces. For records, this isn't a problem — Jackson uses accessor methods automatically.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Spring Boot includes Jackson as the default JSON processor. When you return an object from a RestController method, Spring automatically serializes it to JSON using Jackson's ObjectMapper. The ObjectMapper uses reflection to find getter methods and converts each field to JSON properties. For incoming requests, you annotate the parameter with RequestBody, and Jackson deserializes the JSON string back to a Java object using the default constructor and setter methods. This all happens behind the scenes — you don't write parsing code. Jackson follows JavaBean conventions: it looks for methods like getUserId to serialize the userId field. If you're using Java records, Jackson uses the canonical constructor instead of setters. You can customize behavior with annotations. JsonProperty renames fields — useful when your API uses snake case like order underscore id but your Java code uses camelCase. JsonIgnore excludes sensitive fields like passwords from responses. One thing that surprises freshers: Jackson ignores extra JSON fields by default. If the client sends a field not in your Java class, Jackson doesn't throw an error — it just skips it. For dates, Spring Boot configures Jackson to serialize LocalDateTime as ISO eight-six-zero-one strings automatically. If you need a custom date format, use JsonFormat to specify the pattern.

question: What is the difference between JSON serialization and deserialization?
title: JSON Serialization vs Deserialization
direct_answer: Serialization converts a Java object to JSON string for sending in HTTP responses. Deserialization converts a JSON string back to a Java object for processing incoming requests. In Spring Boot, Jackson handles both automatically through HttpMessageConverter.

interviewer_intent.testing: Clear understanding of the bidirectional data conversion pipeline in REST APIs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing which direction is which, or not knowing that @RestController triggers serialization automatically
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention custom JsonSerializer and JsonDeserializer for types Jackson can't handle by default, like legacy date formats

sections.title: Two Directions of JSON Conversion
sections.content:
**Serialization** is the process of converting a **Java object** into a **JSON string** so it can be sent over HTTP in a response. **Deserialization** is the reverse: converting an **incoming JSON string** into a **Java object** so your code can work with it. Think of serialization as **Java to JSON** (outbound) and deserialization as **JSON to Java** (inbound).

In Spring Boot, Jackson's **ObjectMapper** handles both directions automatically through **HttpMessageConverter**. When a @RestController method returns an object, Spring serializes it. When a method parameter has **@RequestBody**, Spring deserializes the incoming request body. This bidirectional pipeline is invisible to you as a developer — no manual parsing, no string manipulation. Both processes use **reflection** to inspect the object structure and match fields to JSON properties.

sections.title: JSON Serialization vs Deserialization at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Serialization|~Java object to JSON string, happens automatically when RestController returns an object
blue|Deserialization|~JSON string to Java object, triggered by RequestBody annotation on method parameters
emerald|HttpMessageConverter|~Spring's interface that delegates to Jackson for JSON conversion in both directions
violet|Reflection-based|~Jackson inspects object structure at runtime using reflection to map fields to JSON
rose|Custom serializers|~extend JsonSerializer for types Jackson can't handle, like legacy date formats or custom enums
cyan|ObjectMapper|~the central Jackson class that orchestrates both serialization and deserialization

sections.title: When Custom Serializers and Deserializers Are Needed
sections.content:
Use default Jackson behavior for **standard Java types** like String, Integer, List, LocalDateTime — it handles these out of the box. Write a **custom JsonSerializer** when you need to format data in a non-standard way, like converting a BigDecimal price to a string with exactly two decimal places and a currency symbol. Write a **custom JsonDeserializer** when parsing **legacy date formats** that don't match ISO 8601, like MM-slash-dd-slash-yyyy from an old system.

Use custom serializers for **enums** when you want the JSON value to differ from the enum name — for example, serializing OrderStatus.PENDING_PAYMENT as pending underscore payment in snake case. Register custom serializers globally in an ObjectMapper configuration class so they apply across your entire application.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing the direction**: Freshers say serialization when they mean deserialization or vice versa. Remember: serialize is to make a serial (JSON string) from an object. Deserialize is to reconstruct the object from the string.
- **Not knowing RestController triggers serialization**: Freshers think they need to manually call ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString in controller methods. Spring Boot does this automatically for RestController return values — you just return the object.
- **Forgetting RequestBody for deserialization**: Freshers write a POST endpoint with a plain parameter (not annotated with RequestBody) and wonder why the object is null. Without RequestBody, Spring doesn't know to deserialize the request body.

sections.title: Spring Boot Example
Key Points
content: **Serialization**: Java object to JSON string, happens automatically when RestController returns an object
**Deserialization**: JSON string to Java object, triggered by RequestBody annotation on method parameters
**HttpMessageConverter**: Spring's interface that delegates to Jackson for JSON conversion in both directions
**Reflection-based**: Jackson inspects object structure at runtime using reflection to map fields to JSON
**Custom serializers**: extend JsonSerializer for types Jackson can't handle, like legacy date formats or custom enums
**ObjectMapper**: the central Jackson class that orchestrates both serialization and deserialization
**Bidirectional**: most Spring Boot APIs use both directions — deserialize incoming POST data, serialize outgoing responses

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Serialization converts a Java object to a JSON string. Deserialization converts a JSON string back to a Java object. Serialization happens when your RestController returns an object — Spring Boot's Jackson library automatically converts it to JSON for the HTTP response. Deserialization happens when you annotate a method parameter with RequestBody — Jackson reads the incoming JSON and constructs your Java object. Think of serialization as outbound and deserialization as inbound. For serialization, Jackson uses getter methods to read field values. For deserialization, Jackson uses the default constructor and setter methods to populate the object. This all happens automatically through HttpMessageConverter. You don't call ObjectMapper manually. One mistake freshers make is forgetting to add getters — Jackson can't serialize private fields without them, so you get empty JSON. Another is creating a class with only a parameterized constructor — Jackson needs a no-arg constructor for deserialization. Records avoid this because they have accessor methods and a canonical constructor built in. If you want to stand out, mention that you can write custom JsonSerializer classes for types Jackson doesn't handle well. For example, a legacy system might send dates as month-slash-day-slash-year strings. You'd write a custom deserializer to parse that format into LocalDate. You register it globally in your ObjectMapper configuration so it applies everywhere.

question: How do you validate JSON request bodies in Spring Boot?
title: Request Body Validation in Spring Boot
direct_answer: Use Bean Validation (JSR-380) annotations like @NotNull, @NotBlank, @Size, @Email on DTO fields, and add @Valid on the @RequestBody parameter. Spring automatically validates and throws MethodArgumentNotValidException on failure, which you handle with @ControllerAdvice to return structured error responses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of input validation — critical for API security and preventing bad data from entering the system
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Validating only in the service layer or not returning field-level error details to the client
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show you handle MethodArgumentNotValidException with @ControllerAdvice to return a structured error response with field-level details

sections.title: Input Validation with Bean Validation
sections.content:
**Bean Validation** (JSR-380) is the Java standard for validating object fields using annotations like **@NotNull**, **@NotBlank**, **@Size**, and **@Email**.

In Spring Boot, you add these annotations to your **DTO fields**, then annotate the **@RequestBody parameter** with **@Valid**. Spring intercepts the request, runs the validation before your controller method executes, and throws **MethodArgumentNotValidException** if validation fails. This happens **automatically** — you don't write if-else checks in your controller.

The key benefit: validation logic is **declarative** and lives with the data structure, not scattered in service methods. This prevents **invalid data** from entering your system at the API boundary. Think of validation as a gatekeeper: bad data gets rejected with a clear error message before it reaches your business logic or database. To complete the flow, you handle the exception with **@ControllerAdvice** to return a **structured error response** with field-level details like which field failed and why.

sections.title: Validating JSON Request with Bean Validation
When to Validate at the API Layer
sections.content:
Validate at the **API layer** (controller) for **format and structure** checks: is the email valid, is the username not blank, is the age within range. This is your first line of defense against malformed input. Validate at the **service layer** for **business rules** that require database lookups or context: does this username already exist, does the user have permission to perform this action, is this product in stock.

Use **@Valid** on nested objects when your DTO contains other DTOs — for example, an order request with an embedded address object.

Use **custom validators** (implementing ConstraintValidator) for complex rules like "end date must be after start date" that span multiple fields. Always return **field-level error details** to the client — generic "validation failed" messages frustrate frontend developers who need to highlight specific input fields.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Validating only in the service layer**: Freshers put validation logic in service methods, mixing business rules with format checks. This lets bad data reach the service layer and makes testing harder. Validate format at the controller with Bean Validation, then validate business rules in the service.
- **Not returning field-level errors**: Freshers catch MethodArgumentNotValidException and return a generic "Bad Request" message. Clients need to know which field failed ("email is invalid") to show inline error messages in the UI. Extract field errors from BindingResult.
- **Forgetting Valid annotation**: Freshers add NotNull annotations to DTO fields but forget to put Valid on the RequestBody parameter. Spring never runs validation, and invalid data slips through.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Bean Validation JSR-380**: Java standard for declarative validation using annotations like NotNull, NotBlank, Size, Email
**@Valid**: annotation on RequestBody parameter that triggers automatic validation before controller method runs
**MethodArgumentNotValidException**: thrown automatically by Spring when validation fails, contains BindingResult with error details
**@ControllerAdvice**: global exception handler where you catch validation exceptions and return structured error responses
**Field-level errors**: extract from BindingResult to return JSON like field colon email comma message colon Invalid email format
**Validation groups**: advanced feature to run different validation rules for create vs update operations on the same DTO
**Custom validators**: implement ConstraintValidator for complex rules that span multiple fields or require external checks

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You validate JSON request bodies using Bean Validation annotations. On your DTO fields, you add annotations like NotNull for required fields, NotBlank for strings that can't be empty, Size for length constraints, and Email for email format. Then on the controller method parameter, you add Valid along with RequestBody. Spring automatically runs validation before your method executes. If validation fails, Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException. You don't write if-else checks — it's all declarative. The key part is handling the exception properly. You create a ControllerAdvice class with an ExceptionHandler method for MethodArgumentNotValidException. Inside, you extract the field errors from BindingResult and return a structured error response. For example, JSON with fieldErrors as a map: email colon Invalid email format, password colon Must be at least eight characters. This gives the client specific details so they can highlight the problem fields in the UI. One mistake freshers make is validating only in the service layer. That lets bad data get past the controller, and it mixes format checks with business logic. Validate format at the API boundary with Bean Validation. Validate business rules like does this username already exist in the service layer. Another mistake is forgetting the Valid annotation. You add NotNull to fields but don't put Valid on the RequestBody parameter, so Spring never runs validation. To stand out, mention that you use custom validators for complex rules. For example, a StartBeforeEnd validator that checks endDate is after startDate. You implement ConstraintValidator and register it as a Spring bean.

beats.text: Bean Validation (Jakarta Validation, formerly JSR-380) is a standard for declaring constraints on Java fields using annotations. You put constraint annotations on your DTO class and add @Valid to the @RequestBody parameter. Spring validates the incoming JSON before your method body runs.

Without validation at the API layer, invalid data reaches your service and database. A missing required field or a negative age could cause a cryptic NullPointerException deep inside your code rather than a clean 400 or 422 response with a helpful message.

items: @NotNull: field must not be null
@NotBlank: string must not be null, empty, or whitespace
@Size(min=2, max=100): string or collection length bounds
@Email: valid email format
@Min(0) @Max(150): numeric range
@Pattern(regexp = "..."): custom regex for things like phone numbers
@Valid on @RequestBody parameter triggers validation; missing it means constraints are silently ignored

title: DTO vs Entity in REST APIs
direct_answer: An Entity maps to a database table and is managed by JPA with annotations like @Entity and @Id. A DTO (Data Transfer Object) is a plain Java class used to send and receive data over the API. Using separate DTOs prevents over-exposing database structure, avoids JPA lazy loading issues, and gives you control over API shape independent of database schema.

interviewer_intent.testing: Architecture awareness — understanding the separation between persistence layer and API layer
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning @Entity objects directly from controllers, which exposes internal structure and causes LazyInitializationException with lazy-loaded fields
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention MapStruct or ModelMapper for automatic DTO-Entity conversion, and explain JSON infinite recursion with bidirectional JPA relationships

sections.title: Why DTOs and Entities Serve Different Purposes
sections.content:
An **Entity** is a Java class annotated with **@Entity** that maps to a **database table**. JPA (Java Persistence API) manages its lifecycle, tracking changes and syncing with the database.

A **DTO** (Data Transfer Object) is a **plain Java class** (often a **record**) used to carry data between your API and clients. The critical architectural principle: **never expose entities directly through REST endpoints**. Returning an entity in a @RestController response exposes your **internal database structure** — field names, relationships, even internal IDs you don't want clients to know. DTOs give you **control over API shape**: you decide which fields to include, rename database columns to client-friendly names, and flatten nested relationships. DTOs also prevent **LazyInitializationException** when JPA tries to load lazy-loaded collections outside the transaction. Think of entities as your persistence layer's private language, and DTOs as your API layer's public contract.

rows: No JPA involvement, safe to serialize

sections.title: When to Use DTOs vs Entities
sections.content:
Use **entities** in the **repository and service layers** for database operations — saving, querying, updating records. Never return entities from **@RestController methods** — always convert to DTOs first.

Use **DTOs** for all **API request and response bodies**. Create separate request and response DTOs even for the same resource when they differ — for example, CreateUserRequest has a password field, but UserResponse doesn't.

Use DTOs to **flatten complex relationships**: if your Order entity has a nested Customer entity, your OrderResponse DTO might include just customerId and customerName as flat fields.

Use **mapping libraries** like **MapStruct** or **ModelMapper** to automate entity-to-DTO conversion instead of writing manual mapping code. This keeps your service layer clean and reduces boilerplate.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Returning entities directly from controllers**: Freshers return an Entity object from a RestController method. This exposes internal database structure, includes fields like createdDate or version that clients don't need, and risks LazyInitializationException if the entity has lazy-loaded collections. Always map to a DTO first.
- **Infinite recursion with bidirectional relationships**: Freshers have an Order entity with a list of OrderItem entities, and each OrderItem has a back-reference to Order. Jackson tries to serialize the Order, which serializes the items, which serialize their orders, and so on infinitely, crashing with StackOverflowError. Use DTOs to break the cycle by not including back-references.
- **Over-using entities in request bodies**: Freshers use an Entity class annotated with RequestBody for POST requests. This exposes JPA annotations to the API layer and lets clients send fields like id or createdDate that should be server-controlled. Use a dedicated request DTO.

sections.title: Spring Boot Example
Key Points
content: **Entity**: JPA-managed class that maps to a database table, used in repository and service layers
**DTO**: plain data carrier for API requests and responses, no JPA annotations or persistence tracking
**Separation of concerns**: entities represent database structure, DTOs represent API contract — keep them separate
**Lazy loading issues**: entities with lazy collections cause LazyInitializationException when serialized outside a transaction
**Infinite recursion**: bidirectional JPA relationships cause Jackson to loop infinitely when serializing entities directly
**MapStruct**: code-generation library that automates entity-to-DTO mapping with compile-time type safety
**API evolution**: using DTOs lets you change the API shape without altering the database schema or vice versa

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: An entity is a JPA-managed class that maps to a database table. You annotate it with Entity and Id, and JPA tracks changes to sync with the database. A DTO is a plain Java class, often a record, that you use to send and receive data over the API. The key principle is never return entities directly from RestController methods. If you do, you expose your internal database structure to clients. They see field names, relationships, even internal IDs you don't want to expose. Plus, if the entity has lazy-loaded collections, Jackson will try to serialize them outside the transaction and you'll get LazyInitializationException. DTOs solve this. In your service layer, you load the entity from the database, then map it to a DTO before returning to the controller. The DTO contains only the fields you want in the API response. You can rename fields, flatten nested objects, and exclude sensitive data. For example, a User entity might have a password hash field, but your UserResponse DTO doesn't include it. Another problem with entities is infinite recursion. If you have an Order entity with a list of OrderItems, and each OrderItem has a back-reference to the Order, Jackson loops infinitely trying to serialize them. Using DTOs breaks the cycle because you don't include the back-reference. One mistake freshers make is using entities as request bodies. They annotate the entity with RequestBody for a POST endpoint. This exposes JPA annotations to the API layer and lets clients send fields they shouldn't control, like id or createdDate. Use a dedicated request DTO instead. To stand out, mention MapStruct or ModelMapper for automatic entity-to-DTO conversion. Instead of writing manual mapping code, MapStruct generates it at compile time based on matching field names. This keeps your service layer clean and makes refactoring safer.

groups.label: Entity
groups.text: A JPA-managed class that maps to a database table. It lives in the persistence layer, carries JPA annotations like @Id and @OneToMany, and may have lazy-loaded collections.

groups.label: DTO (Data Transfer Object)
groups.text: A plain Java class (or record) designed purely for API data exchange. It has no JPA annotations, contains only what the client needs to see or send, and can be validated with Bean Validation.

items: Always use a DTO at the controller layer — never return an @Entity directly from @RestController
Use separate request DTOs (CreateTaskRequest) and response DTOs (TaskResponse) to control exactly what comes in and what goes out

beats.text: Task entity has a User owner with @ManyToOne and User has a List of Tasks with @OneToMany — bidirectional. Return the entity from @GetMapping and Jackson serializes Task, then User, then User's tasks, then each task's user, then... stack overflow. The fix: a TaskResponse DTO with just {id, title, done, ownerName} — no JPA relationships, no recursion. Conversion from Entity to DTO is done in the service layer using manual mapping or MapStruct, which generates the code at compile time. production trap: @JsonIgnore on entity fields is a band-aid, not a fix. It couples your JPA model to your API contract. Use proper DTOs.

speakable_v2.cap: Entity = database concern. DTO = API concern. Never mix them. Return DTOs from controllers. Map Entity to DTO in the service layer. Use MapStruct for zero-boilerplate mapping.
